As another example: C and D are events in S, with P(C) = 0.6, P(D) = 0.5, and P(C ∪ D) =
0.8. Are C and D independent?
We must find P(C ∩ D), and we know that P(C ∪ D) = P(C) + P(D) – P(C ∪ D). Therefore,
0.8 = 0.6 + 0.5 – P(C ∩ D), and P(C ∩ D) = 0.3. Then P(C ∩ D) = 0.3 = 0.6 * 0.5 = P(C) *
P(D), so the events C and D are independent.

8.1 i ntroduction
Having defined elementary operations and laws for probability, our next objective is the
development of the tools for describing and studying different types of experiments. Before
embarking on a study of various types of experiments, however, we must first study the
generic concept of a probability distribution and the related toolkit; this topic is pursued in
this and the next several chapters.

appear. Equally likely outcomes for this experiment are triples of H’s and T’s, and from them
we can see that these probabilities hold:

What we have done is associate a number (0, 1, 2, or 3) with each outcome in the sample
space. HHH has “3” attached to it. When we perform the experiment, an outcome will occur,
and with it, the number of that outcome. This is an example of a random variable:
A random variable is a numerical quantity whose value is determined by a random
experiment.
That is, a random variable is a mapping from the sample space S to the set of real numbers R.
When an outcome occurs, the random variable takes on the value attached to that outcome.
Here are some examples.
1. In the above experiment, let the random variable X be the number of heads.
2. Roll two dice; let the random variable Y be the total number of dots on the upper faces.
3. Inspect 20 items out of a production lot of 1,000; let Z be the number of items that
fail the inspection.
4. Select a city at random from the Cost of Living file discussed in the previous chapter;
let X be the number of cities with low transportation index values.
5. Flip a coin until the first head appears; let Y be the number of trials before the first head.
In each of these examples, the random variable can take on only certain exact values. Such
random variables are called discrete, and are defined in this way:
A random variable is discrete if the set of its possible values, called the range or
space of the random variable, is finite or countably infinite.
c H a P ter 8 n p robab I l I ty t oolk I t n n n 89
In Example 5, the range of the random variable is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, …, and is countably
infinite.
A random variable is continuous if it can assume any real value in an interval; that
is, its range is an interval.
These are examples of continuous random variables:
1. Let X be the height of a randomly chosen person.
2. Let Y be the time required to perform some task.
3. Let Z be the distance required to stop a car traveling at 50 mph.
In these experiments, the random variables can take on any value within an interval of values,
though in practice we might approximate them with discrete random variables.
For now, we will consider discrete random variables, then extend the concepts we develop
to the continuous case.

8.6 i ndependent r andom v ariables
We have seen that when two events A and B are independent, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) ∗ P(B), and
the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other. We can extend this con-
cept to include random variables:
The random variables X and Y are independent if, for all possible values of X and Y,
P(X = x and Y = y) = P(X = x) ∗ P(Y = y).
That is, any pair of events (X = x) and (Y = y) is independent; the value taken on by one of the
random variables has no effect on the probability of the other.
Rolling two dice provides us with an example of a pair of independent random variables.
Let X be the number of dots on the upper face of the first die, and let Y be the number of
dots on the upper face of the second. Since there is no physical connection between the
two dice, it seems reasonable that these random variables should be independent, and a
check of the 36 pairs of nontrivial events of the form “(X = x) and (Y = y)” will show that
this is so.

9.1 i ntroduction
Probability distributions arise in a variety of situations in the real world, and many of these dis-
tributions fall into a relatively small number of categories. Investigations of these distributions
will provide powerful tools for analyzing the natural systems in which they correspond. We
will be able to construct mathematical models of real-world systems incorporating these prob-
ability distributions, and to describe and predict the behavior of the systems through analysis
of the models. In this chapter, we will provide an overview of discrete probability distributions.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 9.2 Problem s olving through Modeling
chunks.content:
9.2 Problem s olving through Modeling
In this chapter, we will use deductive logic, reasoning from the whole to a part, rather than the
inductive logic we apply in statistical inference. Probability distributions will be constructed
as models of populations, and we will find probabilities of events within those populations.
Corresponding to each population, the model will consist of a type of probability distribution
with the mean and variance of the associated random variable.
Figure 9.1 illustrates the process of solving a real-world problem through the application of
such a probability model. This process is composed of these steps:
1. From the real-world problem, identify the appropriate type of probability model.
2. Using values from the real-world problem, describe the parameters of the probability.
3. Find a solution to the model, and examine its plausibility in terms of the model. If the
solution is unreasonable, repeat this step.
4. From the solution of the model, find the corresponding solution to the original prob-
lem and consider its plausibility. If the real-world solution is unreasonable, reconsider
step 2 and continue.

There are two ways in which this process can fail. First, the solution of the model may be
incorrect; this type of error generally is easily found and easily corrected. Second, the model
itself may not correspond sufficiently to the real-world problem to provide an adequate rep-
resentation of its relevant features. This will render incorrect any solution based on the
model. This type of error is more subtle than the first and requires modifying or replacing
the model.
All figures and tables in this chapter appear on the companion DVD.
The Dartmouth/Thayer approach to solving engineering problems, proposed by Dartmouth
College’s Thayer School of Engineering, is another perspective on problem solving that
requires students to work in teams and develop critical thinking skills while using written
and oral communication skills. This problem-solving technique consists of 10 steps: state
the problem, redefine the problem, identify constraints and general specifications, identify a
first set of alternative solutions, select an alternative, redefine the problem using the selected
alternative, refine and add specifications, brainstorm to generate other possible alternatives,
develop a new set of specifications, and select the most viable alternative.
1
A general approach to problem solving that is useful in this subject is an iterative approach
that involves brainstorming, constructing models, analyzing, and testing until an acceptable
solution is reached. It is important that all steps be done in order. These steps are:
1. State the problem.
Enter the creative problem-solving cycle with a statement of a problem that pertains to a
specific topic. The problem may take the form of an open-ended question or an existing
condition in need of change.
2. Redefine the problem.
The problem solvers should assume that the initial problem comes to them reflecting the
bias of their customer and also his preconceived notion(s) of a desired solution. Therefore,
the problem solvers must question the customer and redefine the problem in a “cleaner”
form. The new problem statement is less ambiguous; it is open-ended and not constrained
by the customer’s preconceived ideas.
3. Identify constraints and set general specifications.
Once the problem solvers have a clear understanding of the customer and his needs, brain-
storming will help generate a list of specifications that will establish the constraints the solu-
tion must meet. Some constraints (moral, legal, ethical) may apply to any problem, not just
this one.
The first time through the cycle, the specifications will be general in nature. For optimal

4. Identify alternative solutions.
Brainstorm possible solutions to the problem using established specifications and constraints.
Brainstorming is a free flow of ideas without criticism, since this would hinder tapping into
the group’s innate creativity. A long list assures the problem solvers that another solution can
be found should a first or second choice fail.
5. Select the most viable alternative.

7. Refine and add specifications.
Brainstorm to develop refined specifications for the alternative selected. In this second itera-
tion, the specifications should be more specifically defined, quantified, and justified relative
to the alternative solution that has been chosen.
8. Brainstorm alternatives.
Using the refined and more-focused specifications, additional appropriate alternatives
should be generated.
9. Reiterate until the problem is solved.
10. Select the most viable alternative.
